**Frederick Jacob Titus Chiluba** (30 April 1943 – 18 June 2011) was a [Zambian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zambia "Zambia") politician who was the second [president of Zambia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Zambia "President of Zambia") from 1991 to 2002. Chiluba, a trade union leader, won the country's multi-party presidential election in 1991 as the candidate of the [Movement for Multi-party Democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movement_for_Multi-party_Democracy "Movement for Multi-party Democracy") (MMD), defeating long-time President [Kenneth Kaunda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Kaunda "Kenneth Kaunda"). He was re-elected in 1996. As he was unable to run for a third term in 2001, former Vice President [Levy Mwanawasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levy_Mwanawasa "Levy Mwanawasa") instead ran as the MMD candidate and succeeded him. After leaving office, Chiluba was the subject of a long investigation and trial regarding alleged corruption; he was eventually acquitted in 2009.

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frederick_Chiluba&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Chiluba was born to Jacob Titus Chiluba Nkonde and Diana Kaimba and grew up in Luapula Province where he was born. He did his basic education at Mambilima Mbolo Special School and his secondary education at Kawambwa Boys Technical Secondary School in [Kawambwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kawambwa "Kawambwa"), where he was expelled in the second year for political activities. He became a bus conductor, and later a politician.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-bbcprofile-2) He worked as a city councilor before becoming an accounts assistant at Atlas Copco. He later joined the National Union of Building.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frederick_Chiluba&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Chiluba and his second wife, former [First Lady of Zambia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Lady_of_Zambia "First Lady of Zambia")[Vera Tembo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vera_Tembo "Vera Tembo"), with whom he had nine children, divorced in 2000 after 33 years of marriage.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-independent-1) Tembo has gone on to pursue a political career of her own, becoming MMD Chairperson for Women's Affairs, being elected to the Zambian Parliament, and becoming deputy [Minister of the Environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_the_Environment "Minister of the Environment") in 2006.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-3) On 6 May 2002, Chiluba married his third wife, [Regina Mwanza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regina_Mwanza?action=edit&redlink=1 "Regina Mwanza (page does not exist)"), the former chairperson of women's affairs for the [Movement for Multi-Party Democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movement_for_Multi-Party_Democracy "Movement for Multi-Party Democracy") (MMD), in Lusaka.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-russell-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-allafrica-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-zpost-6)

Chiluba's personal appearance and dapper dress as well as his short stature (he stood 1.5 m (5 ft) tall) was commented on both by his supporters and opponents throughout his career.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-russell-4)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-7) In connection with European corruption allegations against him in the late 2000s, it was revealed that a Swiss shop had produced over 100 pairs of size 6 shoes for him with two inch heels, many monogrammed.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-8)

His careful appearance and taste for fine suits became a trademark,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-bbcprofile-2) and was noted during his corruption trial. Roy Clarke, writing in _[The Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Post\_(Zambia) "The Post (Zambia)")_, ran a recurring column which lampooned the President during his time in office as "a vain, cross-dressing, high-heel wearing, adulterous, dwarf thief".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-9) Political opponents made reference to these charges and traits in their criticisms of Chiluba's rule. Candidate [Michael Sata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Sata "Michael Sata"), for instance, said "Chiluba's thinking is as tall as he is... We are not going to steal money, we are not going to plunder, we are not going to buy suits, we are not going to buy shoes. We are not going to give girls houses..."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-10) Kaunda referred to Chiluba as the "Four-foot Dwarf" during Chiluba's rise in opposition politics.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-11) Chiluba was acquitted of all corruption charges in August 2009.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-12) Chiluba had also been described by the BBC as "a fervent [born-again Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Born-again_Christian "Born-again Christian") [whose] private life was the subject of much gossip."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-bbcprofile-2)

## Unions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frederick_Chiluba&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Unions")]

Chiluba went on to win the chairmanship of the [Zambia Congress of Trade Unions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zambia_Congress_of_Trade_Unions "Zambia Congress of Trade Unions") (ZCTU).[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-13) He and several leaders in ZCTU were detained in 1981 by President Kenneth Kaunda for calling a wildcat strike that paralyzed most of the Zambian economy. The union leaders were released after a judge ruled their detention as unconstitutional. In 1987, he successfully withstood challenge to his chairmanship of NUBEGW that would have put his ZCTU position in jeopardy.

## Politics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frederick_Chiluba&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Politics")]

In 1990, soon after UNIP gave up its monopoly on power, he helped form the [Movement for Multiparty Democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movement_for_Multiparty_Democracy "Movement for Multiparty Democracy") (MMD), and became its presidential candidate in the snap 1991 election called as part of the deal that ended one-party rule. Due in part to festering resentment at UNIP's 25-year rule (including 17 years as the only legal party), Chiluba defeated Kaunda in a massive landslide, taking 75 percent of the vote to Kaunda's 25 percent–the second-biggest margin of victory for a contested election in Zambian history. Chiluba took office on 2 November of that year. On 29 December 1991, he declared Zambia a Christian nation. This declaration was included in the 2016 Constitutional Amendment Bill which is part of the current Constitution of the Republic of Zambia. He won re-election to a second five-year term in 1996 despite a lawsuit questioning his birthplace and hence his eligibility for the post.

Chiluba attempted to deport Kaunda on the grounds that he was a [Malawian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malawi "Malawi"). He amended the constitution in order to stop citizens with foreign parentage from standing for the presidency, aimed at disqualifying Kaunda.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-15) His attempt to deport Kaunda was unsuccessful as Kaunda's Zambian citizenship was confirmed by the _[Lewanika and Others vs. Chiluba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewanika\_and\_Others\_vs.\_Chiluba "Lewanika and Others vs. Chiluba")_ Supreme Court ruling in 2000.

Some candidates in the [1996 presidential elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_Zambian_presidential_election "1996 Zambian presidential election") challenged his eligibility on these grounds, claiming that he or his real father was born in [Zaire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zaire "Zaire"). However, he was raised in the Copperbelt of Zambia and this contributed to his taking up of unionism.

In 1997 his government survived a [coup attempt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_Zambian_coup_d'%C3%A9tat_attempt "1997 Zambian coup d'état attempt") after which Chiluba immediately declared a state of emergency and began jailing, without charges, persons suspected of involvement in the coup. These included several Zambian politicians, including those from opposition parties and the country's previous President, [Kenneth Kaunda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Kaunda "Kenneth Kaunda").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-16)

In late 2001, Chiluba divorced his second wife, Vera, with whom he had nine children, namely Helen, Miko, Hortensia, Castro, Chongo, Kaindu, Huldah, Frederick Jr and Verocia . With his first wife he had Tito and Nikombe.

He later married the MMD Women's Chairperson, Regina Mwanza a divorcee. Despite his party's overwhelming majority in parliament, he failed to win support in his bid to amend the constitution allowing him to run for a third term. No member of parliament ever moved the motion in the house to amend the national constitution, the government never presented any paper on the matter nor was there any referendum to amend the national constitution. The third term debate was between different groups within and outside the MMD. Chiluba himself was quiet about it. He stepped down at the end of his term on 2 January 2002, and was replaced by [Levy Mwanawasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levy_Mwanawasa "Levy Mwanawasa"), his one-time vice-president. Chiluba started out as a [socialist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist "Socialist"), but accepted some economic reforms.

Chiluba can be said to have left both an economic and a political legacy.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-17) Economically he started the process of ending Zambia's socialist [command economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Command_economy "Command economy"). He presided over various economic reforms. He worked closely with British Prime Minister [John Major](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Major "John Major") throughout the early 1990s to reduce Zambia's debt.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-18) Major and Chiluba restructured Zambia's debt to Britain which allowed Zambia to begin paying off debts to other foreign countries without their credit being negatively affected. This was considered the most successful [debt restructuring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debt_restructuring "Debt restructuring") Africa during the 1990s.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-19)

Chiluba opposed international economic institutions. His successor [Levy Mwanawasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levy_Mwanawasa "Levy Mwanawasa") re-established relations with [IMF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Monetary_Fund "International Monetary Fund") and [World Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Bank "World Bank") which had been abolished during Chiluba's government.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] This view contradicts Chiluba's economic reforms which included the Privatisation of Parastatals which he spearheaded with close cooperation with the World Bank and the IMF. Chiluba is also credited with kickstarting the privatisation of ZCCM (Zambia Consolidatited Copper Mines) in the late 1990s, the country's crown jewel.

## Corruption

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frederick_Chiluba&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Corruption")]

After leaving office, Chiluba was a target of Mwanawasa's campaign against corruption: in February 2003, he was charged along with his former intelligence chief, [Xavier Chungu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Chungu?action=edit&redlink=1 "Xavier Chungu (page does not exist)"), and several former ministers and senior officials, with 168 counts of theft totalling more than $40m.

It was alleged that money was diverted from the Ministry of Finance into an account held at the London branch of the [Zambia National Commercial Bank (Zanaco)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zambia_National_Commercial_Bank_(Zanaco)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Zambia National Commercial Bank (Zanaco) (page does not exist)"). Chiluba said the account was used by the country's intelligence services to fund operations abroad. Investigators said it was a slush fund, used to meet Chiluba and Chungu's private and personal expenses.

Most of the charges that were made against him were later dropped, but others remained. In addition, his wife Regina was arrested for receiving stolen goods.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-22)

In early 2006, Chiluba was flown to [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa") for medical attention for a heart condition. After resisting the government's call for him to return to Zambia for what they termed as long-term treatment, he returned on 15 July.

On 4 May 2007 he was found guilty of stealing $46m (£23m) in a civil case by a UK court.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-gregpalastdn-24) London high court judge [Peter Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Smith_(judge) "Peter Smith (judge)") accused Chiluba of shamelessly defrauding his people and flaunting his wealth with an expensive wardrobe of "stupendous proportions".[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-gregpalastdn-24) He also castigated his lawyer, [Iqbal Meer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iqbal_Meer?action=edit&redlink=1 "Iqbal Meer (page does not exist)"), saying "I am satisfied that no honest solicitor in his position would have done what he did." His unquestioning acceptance of the money - transferred to a London bank account by the Zambian intelligence service - was "classic blind eye dishonesty".[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-26) An appeal against the ruling was allowed by the court of appeal in 2008.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-27) Large sections of Zambian society have however questioned Peter Smith's credibility following reprimands and recusals by the British judiciary.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-32) Many have argued that the British Judge should have concentrated on cases pertaining to properties that were allegedly obtained by corrupt means in Britain and Europe rather than properties in Zambia. However, after offering Chiluba's clothes to his family in 2016, the [Anti-Corruption Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Corruption_Commission_zambia?action=edit&redlink=1 "Anti-Corruption Commission zambia (page does not exist)") later secured a judgement in the Supreme Court of Zambia where Chiluba's estate (Tedworth Properties) was forfeited to the state after seizing it in 2002.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-33)

Chiluba, however, continued to plead innocence and refused to recognise the verdict of the Judge Peter Smith who he accused of having been bribed by the Mwanawasa government. It is yet to be seen what effect the civil ruling in the UK will have on the criminal proceedings in the Zambian courts. Chiluba indicated at the time that the judgement in the UK had rendered the criminal proceedings in Zambia academic by heavily prejudicing his case.

On 7 June, the amount, which Chiluba was ordered to repay, was increased to $58m, accounting for interest and legal costs.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-34) Several days later, Judge Smith ordered Chiluba to leave his home in Lusaka within two weeks because it was judged to have been bought with money stolen from the public.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-35)

Chiluba collapsed on 24 May 2007 due to heart trouble and was hospitalized.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-36) He was released from the hospital on 29 May, and on 30 May doctors judged him to be fit to stand trial on the embezzlement charges following an examination.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-37) On 31 May, a court ruled that his trial should proceed, although his lawyers argued that it should not due to his poor health.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-38) The judge rejected arguments from Chiluba's lawyers and doctors that the former president is too sick to face prosecution over graft charges.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-39) On 27 July he was flown to South Africa to be treated for heart trouble;[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-SA-40) this had been approved by the government earlier in the month.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-41) He was scheduled to appear in court for his trial on 14 August,[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-SA-40) and he returned to Zambia on 11 August, saying in an interview that he was "surviving on God's will". His spokesman said that his illness made it uncertain whether he would appear in court; in July, it was ruled that, if necessary, Chiluba would participate in the trial through video or a judge would go to his home.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-42) On 14 August, Chiluba rejected the idea of participating in the trial through video,[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-Back-43) saying that it would be illegal.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-44)

After appearing briefly in court on 14 August, Chiluba was present for the resumption of trial proceedings on 15 August. Chiluba took breaks during the day for health reasons.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-Back-43)

Chiluba's wife Regina was arrested on 3 September for allegedly receiving money and property stolen by Chiluba during his time in office, despite having previously been released after the case against her had been dropped on 24 August. Chiluba and his wife protested the arrest.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-45)

In May 2008, the government announced that it had recovered nearly 60 million dollars in money and assets allegedly stolen during Chiluba's presidency.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-46)

Having long suffered from health problems, Mwanawasa died later in 2008. Chiluba was acquitted on all charges on 17 August 2009.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-47) Scores of people packed the Lusaka Magistrates Court to hear Judge Jones Chinyama final judgement which concluded that Dr. Frederick Chiluba was not guilty of the corruption charges laid against him and hence was acquitted.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-48)

## Political stances after leaving office

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frederick_Chiluba&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Political stances after leaving office")]

Chiluba's relationship with President Mwanawasa and the MMD soured badly after he was charged with corruption. He backed Mwanawasa's main opponent, [Michael Sata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Sata "Michael Sata"), in the [2006 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Zambian_presidential_election "2006 Zambian presidential election"). After Mwanawasa's death in 2008, Vice-president [Rupiah Banda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupiah_Banda "Rupiah Banda") succeeded him and Chiluba's fortunes improved markedly. Chiluba was acquitted in 2009—a decision that Sata alleged was "engineered" by Banda—and President Banda refused to allow the state to appeal the verdict or pursue the matter further. Chiluba announced in January 2010 that he was supporting Banda for re-election in 2011, while also criticising the main opposition leaders. [Transparency International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transparency_International "Transparency International") argued that Chiluba was endorsing Banda "so that he can be guaranteed his freedom", and Sata was similarly critical: "Chiluba will do anything possible to ensure that his friend remains in power."[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-49)

## Death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frederick_Chiluba&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Death")]

Chiluba died of a [heart attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_attack "Heart attack") on 18 June 2011,[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-50)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-lusakatimes.com-51) shortly after midnight. His spokesman, [Emmanuel Mwamba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmanuel_Mwamba "Emmanuel Mwamba"), announced his death. Mwamba stated that Chiluba had a normal day on 17 June, and even had time to meet some of his lawyers. He had later complained of stomach pains.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-lusakatimes.com-51)

**Frederick Jacob Titus Chiluba** (30 April 1943 – 18 June 2011) was a [Zambian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zambia "Zambia") politician who was the second [president of Zambia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Zambia "President of Zambia") from 1991 to 2002. Chiluba, a trade union leader, won the country's multi-party presidential election in 1991 as the candidate of the [Movement for Multi-party Democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movement_for_Multi-party_Democracy "Movement for Multi-party Democracy") (MMD), defeating long-time President [Kenneth Kaunda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Kaunda "Kenneth Kaunda"). He was re-elected in 1996. As he was unable to run for a third term in 2001, former Vice President [Levy Mwanawasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levy_Mwanawasa "Levy Mwanawasa") instead ran as the MMD candidate and succeeded him. After leaving office, Chiluba was the subject of a long investigation and trial regarding alleged corruption; he was eventually acquitted in 2009.

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frederick_Chiluba&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Chiluba was born to Jacob Titus Chiluba Nkonde and Diana Kaimba and grew up in Luapula Province where he was born. He did his basic education at Mambilima Mbolo Special School and his secondary education at Kawambwa Boys Technical Secondary School in [Kawambwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kawambwa "Kawambwa"), where he was expelled in the second year for political activities. He became a bus conductor, and later a politician.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-bbcprofile-2) He worked as a city councilor before becoming an accounts assistant at Atlas Copco. He later joined the National Union of Building.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frederick_Chiluba&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Chiluba and his second wife, former [First Lady of Zambia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Lady_of_Zambia "First Lady of Zambia")[Vera Tembo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vera_Tembo "Vera Tembo"), with whom he had nine children, divorced in 2000 after 33 years of marriage.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-independent-1) Tembo has gone on to pursue a political career of her own, becoming MMD Chairperson for Women's Affairs, being elected to the Zambian Parliament, and becoming deputy [Minister of the Environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_the_Environment "Minister of the Environment") in 2006.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-3) On 6 May 2002, Chiluba married his third wife, [Regina Mwanza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regina_Mwanza?action=edit&redlink=1 "Regina Mwanza (page does not exist)"), the former chairperson of women's affairs for the [Movement for Multi-Party Democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movement_for_Multi-Party_Democracy "Movement for Multi-Party Democracy") (MMD), in Lusaka.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-russell-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-allafrica-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-zpost-6)

Chiluba's personal appearance and dapper dress as well as his short stature (he stood 1.5 m (5 ft) tall) was commented on both by his supporters and opponents throughout his career.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-russell-4)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-7) In connection with European corruption allegations against him in the late 2000s, it was revealed that a Swiss shop had produced over 100 pairs of size 6 shoes for him with two inch heels, many monogrammed.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-8)

His careful appearance and taste for fine suits became a trademark,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-bbcprofile-2) and was noted during his corruption trial. Roy Clarke, writing in _[The Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Post\_(Zambia) "The Post (Zambia)")_, ran a recurring column which lampooned the President during his time in office as "a vain, cross-dressing, high-heel wearing, adulterous, dwarf thief".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-9) Political opponents made reference to these charges and traits in their criticisms of Chiluba's rule. Candidate [Michael Sata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Sata "Michael Sata"), for instance, said "Chiluba's thinking is as tall as he is... We are not going to steal money, we are not going to plunder, we are not going to buy suits, we are not going to buy shoes. We are not going to give girls houses..."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-10) Kaunda referred to Chiluba as the "Four-foot Dwarf" during Chiluba's rise in opposition politics.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-11) Chiluba was acquitted of all corruption charges in August 2009.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-12) Chiluba had also been described by the BBC as "a fervent [born-again Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Born-again_Christian "Born-again Christian") [whose] private life was the subject of much gossip."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-bbcprofile-2)

## Unions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frederick_Chiluba&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Unions")]

Chiluba went on to win the chairmanship of the [Zambia Congress of Trade Unions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zambia_Congress_of_Trade_Unions "Zambia Congress of Trade Unions") (ZCTU).[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-13) He and several leaders in ZCTU were detained in 1981 by President Kenneth Kaunda for calling a wildcat strike that paralyzed most of the Zambian economy. The union leaders were released after a judge ruled their detention as unconstitutional. In 1987, he successfully withstood challenge to his chairmanship of NUBEGW that would have put his ZCTU position in jeopardy.

## Politics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frederick_Chiluba&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Politics")]

In 1990, soon after UNIP gave up its monopoly on power, he helped form the [Movement for Multiparty Democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movement_for_Multiparty_Democracy "Movement for Multiparty Democracy") (MMD), and became its presidential candidate in the snap 1991 election called as part of the deal that ended one-party rule. Due in part to festering resentment at UNIP's 25-year rule (including 17 years as the only legal party), Chiluba defeated Kaunda in a massive landslide, taking 75 percent of the vote to Kaunda's 25 percent–the second-biggest margin of victory for a contested election in Zambian history. Chiluba took office on 2 November of that year. On 29 December 1991, he declared Zambia a Christian nation. This declaration was included in the 2016 Constitutional Amendment Bill which is part of the current Constitution of the Republic of Zambia. He won re-election to a second five-year term in 1996 despite a lawsuit questioning his birthplace and hence his eligibility for the post.

Chiluba attempted to deport Kaunda on the grounds that he was a [Malawian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malawi "Malawi"). He amended the constitution in order to stop citizens with foreign parentage from standing for the presidency, aimed at disqualifying Kaunda.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-15) His attempt to deport Kaunda was unsuccessful as Kaunda's Zambian citizenship was confirmed by the _[Lewanika and Others vs. Chiluba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewanika\_and\_Others\_vs.\_Chiluba "Lewanika and Others vs. Chiluba")_ Supreme Court ruling in 2000.

Some candidates in the [1996 presidential elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_Zambian_presidential_election "1996 Zambian presidential election") challenged his eligibility on these grounds, claiming that he or his real father was born in [Zaire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zaire "Zaire"). However, he was raised in the Copperbelt of Zambia and this contributed to his taking up of unionism.

In 1997 his government survived a [coup attempt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_Zambian_coup_d'%C3%A9tat_attempt "1997 Zambian coup d'état attempt") after which Chiluba immediately declared a state of emergency and began jailing, without charges, persons suspected of involvement in the coup. These included several Zambian politicians, including those from opposition parties and the country's previous President, [Kenneth Kaunda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Kaunda "Kenneth Kaunda").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-16)

In late 2001, Chiluba divorced his second wife, Vera, with whom he had nine children, namely Helen, Miko, Hortensia, Castro, Chongo, Kaindu, Huldah, Frederick Jr and Verocia . With his first wife he had Tito and Nikombe.

He later married the MMD Women's Chairperson, Regina Mwanza a divorcee. Despite his party's overwhelming majority in parliament, he failed to win support in his bid to amend the constitution allowing him to run for a third term. No member of parliament ever moved the motion in the house to amend the national constitution, the government never presented any paper on the matter nor was there any referendum to amend the national constitution. The third term debate was between different groups within and outside the MMD. Chiluba himself was quiet about it. He stepped down at the end of his term on 2 January 2002, and was replaced by [Levy Mwanawasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levy_Mwanawasa "Levy Mwanawasa"), his one-time vice-president. Chiluba started out as a [socialist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist "Socialist"), but accepted some economic reforms.

Chiluba can be said to have left both an economic and a political legacy.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-17) Economically he started the process of ending Zambia's socialist [command economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Command_economy "Command economy"). He presided over various economic reforms. He worked closely with British Prime Minister [John Major](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Major "John Major") throughout the early 1990s to reduce Zambia's debt.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-18) Major and Chiluba restructured Zambia's debt to Britain which allowed Zambia to begin paying off debts to other foreign countries without their credit being negatively affected. This was considered the most successful [debt restructuring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debt_restructuring "Debt restructuring") Africa during the 1990s.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-19)

Chiluba opposed international economic institutions. His successor [Levy Mwanawasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levy_Mwanawasa "Levy Mwanawasa") re-established relations with [IMF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Monetary_Fund "International Monetary Fund") and [World Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Bank "World Bank") which had been abolished during Chiluba's government.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] This view contradicts Chiluba's economic reforms which included the Privatisation of Parastatals which he spearheaded with close cooperation with the World Bank and the IMF. Chiluba is also credited with kickstarting the privatisation of ZCCM (Zambia Consolidatited Copper Mines) in the late 1990s, the country's crown jewel.

## Corruption

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frederick_Chiluba&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Corruption")]

After leaving office, Chiluba was a target of Mwanawasa's campaign against corruption: in February 2003, he was charged along with his former intelligence chief, [Xavier Chungu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Chungu?action=edit&redlink=1 "Xavier Chungu (page does not exist)"), and several former ministers and senior officials, with 168 counts of theft totalling more than $40m.

It was alleged that money was diverted from the Ministry of Finance into an account held at the London branch of the [Zambia National Commercial Bank (Zanaco)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zambia_National_Commercial_Bank_(Zanaco)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Zambia National Commercial Bank (Zanaco) (page does not exist)"). Chiluba said the account was used by the country's intelligence services to fund operations abroad. Investigators said it was a slush fund, used to meet Chiluba and Chungu's private and personal expenses.

Most of the charges that were made against him were later dropped, but others remained. In addition, his wife Regina was arrested for receiving stolen goods.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-22)

In early 2006, Chiluba was flown to [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa") for medical attention for a heart condition. After resisting the government's call for him to return to Zambia for what they termed as long-term treatment, he returned on 15 July.

On 4 May 2007 he was found guilty of stealing $46m (£23m) in a civil case by a UK court.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-gregpalastdn-24) London high court judge [Peter Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Smith_(judge) "Peter Smith (judge)") accused Chiluba of shamelessly defrauding his people and flaunting his wealth with an expensive wardrobe of "stupendous proportions".[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-gregpalastdn-24) He also castigated his lawyer, [Iqbal Meer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iqbal_Meer?action=edit&redlink=1 "Iqbal Meer (page does not exist)"), saying "I am satisfied that no honest solicitor in his position would have done what he did." His unquestioning acceptance of the money - transferred to a London bank account by the Zambian intelligence service - was "classic blind eye dishonesty".[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-26) An appeal against the ruling was allowed by the court of appeal in 2008.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-27) Large sections of Zambian society have however questioned Peter Smith's credibility following reprimands and recusals by the British judiciary.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-32) Many have argued that the British Judge should have concentrated on cases pertaining to properties that were allegedly obtained by corrupt means in Britain and Europe rather than properties in Zambia. However, after offering Chiluba's clothes to his family in 2016, the [Anti-Corruption Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Corruption_Commission_zambia?action=edit&redlink=1 "Anti-Corruption Commission zambia (page does not exist)") later secured a judgement in the Supreme Court of Zambia where Chiluba's estate (Tedworth Properties) was forfeited to the state after seizing it in 2002.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-33)

Chiluba, however, continued to plead innocence and refused to recognise the verdict of the Judge Peter Smith who he accused of having been bribed by the Mwanawasa government. It is yet to be seen what effect the civil ruling in the UK will have on the criminal proceedings in the Zambian courts. Chiluba indicated at the time that the judgement in the UK had rendered the criminal proceedings in Zambia academic by heavily prejudicing his case.

On 7 June, the amount, which Chiluba was ordered to repay, was increased to $58m, accounting for interest and legal costs.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-34) Several days later, Judge Smith ordered Chiluba to leave his home in Lusaka within two weeks because it was judged to have been bought with money stolen from the public.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-35)

Chiluba collapsed on 24 May 2007 due to heart trouble and was hospitalized.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-36) He was released from the hospital on 29 May, and on 30 May doctors judged him to be fit to stand trial on the embezzlement charges following an examination.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-37) On 31 May, a court ruled that his trial should proceed, although his lawyers argued that it should not due to his poor health.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-38) The judge rejected arguments from Chiluba's lawyers and doctors that the former president is too sick to face prosecution over graft charges.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-39) On 27 July he was flown to South Africa to be treated for heart trouble;[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-SA-40) this had been approved by the government earlier in the month.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-41) He was scheduled to appear in court for his trial on 14 August,[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-SA-40) and he returned to Zambia on 11 August, saying in an interview that he was "surviving on God's will". His spokesman said that his illness made it uncertain whether he would appear in court; in July, it was ruled that, if necessary, Chiluba would participate in the trial through video or a judge would go to his home.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-42) On 14 August, Chiluba rejected the idea of participating in the trial through video,[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-Back-43) saying that it would be illegal.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-44)

After appearing briefly in court on 14 August, Chiluba was present for the resumption of trial proceedings on 15 August. Chiluba took breaks during the day for health reasons.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-Back-43)

Chiluba's wife Regina was arrested on 3 September for allegedly receiving money and property stolen by Chiluba during his time in office, despite having previously been released after the case against her had been dropped on 24 August. Chiluba and his wife protested the arrest.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-45)

In May 2008, the government announced that it had recovered nearly 60 million dollars in money and assets allegedly stolen during Chiluba's presidency.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-46)

Having long suffered from health problems, Mwanawasa died later in 2008. Chiluba was acquitted on all charges on 17 August 2009.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-47) Scores of people packed the Lusaka Magistrates Court to hear Judge Jones Chinyama final judgement which concluded that Dr. Frederick Chiluba was not guilty of the corruption charges laid against him and hence was acquitted.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-48)

## Political stances after leaving office

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frederick_Chiluba&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Political stances after leaving office")]

Chiluba's relationship with President Mwanawasa and the MMD soured badly after he was charged with corruption. He backed Mwanawasa's main opponent, [Michael Sata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Sata "Michael Sata"), in the [2006 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Zambian_presidential_election "2006 Zambian presidential election"). After Mwanawasa's death in 2008, Vice-president [Rupiah Banda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupiah_Banda "Rupiah Banda") succeeded him and Chiluba's fortunes improved markedly. Chiluba was acquitted in 2009—a decision that Sata alleged was "engineered" by Banda—and President Banda refused to allow the state to appeal the verdict or pursue the matter further. Chiluba announced in January 2010 that he was supporting Banda for re-election in 2011, while also criticising the main opposition leaders. [Transparency International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transparency_International "Transparency International") argued that Chiluba was endorsing Banda "so that he can be guaranteed his freedom", and Sata was similarly critical: "Chiluba will do anything possible to ensure that his friend remains in power."[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-49)

## Death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Frederick_Chiluba&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Death")]

Chiluba died of a [heart attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_attack "Heart attack") on 18 June 2011,[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-50)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-lusakatimes.com-51) shortly after midnight. His spokesman, [Emmanuel Mwamba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmanuel_Mwamba "Emmanuel Mwamba"), announced his death. Mwamba stated that Chiluba had a normal day on 17 June, and even had time to meet some of his lawyers. He had later complained of stomach pains.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Chiluba#cite_note-lusakatimes.com-51)

General elections were held in [Peru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peru "Peru") on 14 April 1985 to elect the [President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_Peru "List of presidents of Peru") and both houses of the [Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congress_of_the_Republic_of_Peru "Congress of the Republic of Peru").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1985_Peruvian_general_election#cite_note-N1-1)[Alan García](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa "Alan García") of the [American Popular Revolutionary Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Popular_Revolutionary_Alliance "American Popular Revolutionary Alliance") (APRA) won the presidential election with 53.1% of the vote, whilst his party gained a majority in both houses of Congress. It was the first time that an APRA candidate won the presidential election.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1985_Peruvian_general_election#cite_note-2)

The election took place amid economic hardship.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1985_Peruvian_general_election#cite_note-3)

General elections were held in [Peru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peru "Peru") on 14 April 1985 to elect the [President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_Peru "List of presidents of Peru") and both houses of the [Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congress_of_the_Republic_of_Peru "Congress of the Republic of Peru").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1985_Peruvian_general_election#cite_note-N1-1)[Alan García](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa "Alan García") of the [American Popular Revolutionary Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Popular_Revolutionary_Alliance "American Popular Revolutionary Alliance") (APRA) won the presidential election with 53.1% of the vote, whilst his party gained a majority in both houses of Congress. It was the first time that an APRA candidate won the presidential election.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1985_Peruvian_general_election#cite_note-2)

The election took place amid economic hardship.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1985_Peruvian_general_election#cite_note-3)

**Alan Gabriel Ludwig García Pérez**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-3) (Latin American Spanish:[[ˈalaŋ‿ɡaβˈɾjel luðˈwiɣ‿ɣaɾˈsi.a ˈpeɾes]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish"); 23 May 1949 – 17 April 2019) was a Peruvian politician who served as [President of Peru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Peru "President of Peru") for two non-consecutive terms, from 1985 to 1990 and from 2006 to 2011.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-4) He was the second leader of the [American Popular Revolutionary Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Popular_Revolutionary_Alliance "American Popular Revolutionary Alliance") (APRA), and its only member to serve as president.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-:1-5) Mentored by the APRA's founder, [Víctor Raúl Haya de la Torre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V%C3%ADctor_Ra%C3%BAl_Haya_de_la_Torre "Víctor Raúl Haya de la Torre"), he served in the [Constituent Assembly of 1978–1979](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constituent_Assembly_of_Peru "Constituent Assembly of Peru"). Elected to the [Peruvian Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peruvian_Congress "Peruvian Congress") in [1980](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_Peruvian_general_election "1980 Peruvian general election"), he rose to the position of General Secretary of the APRA in 1982, and was elected to the presidency in 1985 in a landslide.

García's first presidential term was marked by a severe economic crisis, social unrest, corruption, and violence. At its conclusion, he was accused and investigated for corruption and [illicit enrichment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illicit_enrichment "Illicit enrichment").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-6) In 1992, he filed for asylum following president [Alberto Fujimori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alberto_Fujimori "Alberto Fujimori")'s self-coup, and exiled himself with his family in Colombia and France for nine years.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-7) In the aftermath of Fujimori's downfall, he made a political comeback as he ran for the presidency in [2001](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Peruvian_general_election "2001 Peruvian general election"), but lost in the second round to [Alejandro Toledo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alejandro_Toledo "Alejandro Toledo").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-8)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-9) In [2006](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Peruvian_general_election "2006 Peruvian general election"), he was again elected president, defeating [Ollanta Humala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ollanta_Humala "Ollanta Humala"), a feat considered a political resurrection due to the failure of his first term.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-10)

Throughout García's second term, Peru experienced a steady economy, becoming Latin America's fastest-growing country in 2008, surpassing [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China") in terms of rising GDP. This economic success was acclaimed as a triumph by world leaders, and poverty declined from 48% to 28% nationally.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-12) In addition, Peru signed [free trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_trade "Free trade") agreements with the United States and China during García's presidency, but accusations of corruption persisted throughout his term and beyond. He was succeeded by Humala in 2011. He withdrew from party politics after failing to advance to the second round of the [2016 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Peruvian_general_election "2016 Peruvian general election"), placing fifth in his bid for a third presidential term under the [Popular Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_Alliance_(Peru) "Popular Alliance (Peru)") coalition between his party and the [Christian People's Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_People's_Party_(Peru) "Christian People's Party (Peru)"), which included former rival [Lourdes Flores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lourdes_Flores "Lourdes Flores") as one of his running mates.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-13) On 17 April 2019, García died from a self-inflicted gunshot to the head as police officers under a prosecutor's orders were preparing to arrest him over matters relating to the [Odebrecht scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Car_Wash#Peru "Operation Car Wash").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-:0-14)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-15)

García is considered one of Peru's most controversial yet talented politicians.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-16) He was known as an immensely charismatic orator,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-17) but a 2017 poll of Peruvians named García and his government the most corrupt.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-18)

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alan_Garc%C3%ADa&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Born in the Maison de Santé Clinic of the [Barranco District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barranco_District "Barranco District") into a middle-class family, García met his father for the first time when he was five due to his father's imprisonment at [El Sexto Prison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Sexto_Prison "El Sexto Prison") for being a member of the [Peruvian Aprista Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peruvian_Aprista_Party "Peruvian Aprista Party").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-bioES-19) His mother founded the party's base in the [Camaná Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caman%C3%A1_Province "Camaná Province") of the [Arequipa Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arequipa_Region "Arequipa Region"). From a very young age, he accompanied his father to party meetings and became acquainted with future leaders of the [American Popular Revolutionary Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Popular_Revolutionary_Alliance "American Popular Revolutionary Alliance") (APRA),[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-britbio-20) such as [Luis Alva Castro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luis_Alva_Castro "Luis Alva Castro") and [Mercedes Cabanillas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercedes_Cabanillas "Mercedes Cabanillas"). At age 14, he was already an immensely talented [orator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orator "Orator") when he first gave a speech in honour of party founder [Víctor Raúl Haya de la Torre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V%C3%ADctor_Ra%C3%BAl_Haya_de_la_Torre "Víctor Raúl Haya de la Torre"), whom he admired and followed until his death.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-bioES-19)

García studied law, first at the [Pontifical Catholic University of Peru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontifical_Catholic_University_of_Peru "Pontifical Catholic University of Peru") and later earning a bachelor's degree from the [National University of San Marcos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_University_of_San_Marcos "National University of San Marcos") in 1971.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-21) A year later, he left Peru for [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain"), where he pursued a doctoral degree in constitutional law under the guidance of [Manuel Fraga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_Fraga "Manuel Fraga"). For years García claimed to have earned the degree; in 2014, however, documents from the university proved he never finished the work for it.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-22) In 1974, he moved to [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France") with other members of the APRA to study at the [Sorbonne Nouvelle University Paris 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sorbonne_Nouvelle_University_Paris_3 "Sorbonne Nouvelle University Paris 3") and the [Institut des Hautes Etudes de l'Amérique latine](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institut%20des%20Hautes%20Etudes%20de%20l'Am%C3%A9rique%20latine "fr:Institut des Hautes Etudes de l'Amérique latine") (IHEAL).[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-bioES-19) After earning a diploma in [sociology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sociology "Sociology") from IHEAL, he was called by [Víctor Raúl Haya de la Torre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V%C3%ADctor_Ra%C3%BAl_Haya_de_la_Torre "Víctor Raúl Haya de la Torre") to come back to Peru in order to run for the [Constituent Assembly election in 1978](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1978_Peruvian_Constituent_Assembly_election "1978 Peruvian Constituent Assembly election"). García was elected a Member of the Assembly, where he impressed his colleagues with his oratory and skillful rhetoric.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-bioES-19) As APRA's Secretary of Organization, he was assigned to conduct the party's public affairs in the wake of Haya de la Torre's death in 1979.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-britbio-20)

From his first marriage, García had one daughter, [Carla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carla_Garc%C3%ADa "Carla García"), who is also active in Peruvian politics since 2014.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-pilarsepa-23) With his second wife Pilar Nores, from whom he separated in 2010,[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-24) García had four children.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-pilarsepa-23) He also had another child from an extramarital affair with economist Roxanne Cheesman.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-pilarsepa-23)

García was elected to [Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congress_of_the_Republic_of_Peru "Congress of the Republic of Peru") in 1980.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-britbio-20) Two years later, he was elected General Secretary of the [Peruvian Aprista Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Popular_Revolutionary_Alliance "American Popular Revolutionary Alliance"). He was elected to serve as president of the Republic in the 1985 general elections.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-britbio-20)

## First presidency (1985–1990)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alan_Garc%C3%ADa&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: First presidency (1985–1990)")]

See also: [First presidency of Alan García](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_presidency_of_Alan_Garc%C3%ADa "First presidency of Alan García")

García won the presidential election on 14 April 1985 with 45% of the votes. Since he did not receive the 50% of the votes required for a first-round victory, a runoff was scheduled between him and [Alfonso Barrantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_Barrantes_Ling%C3%A1n "Alfonso Barrantes Lingán") (the former mayor of Lima) of the [United Left](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Left_(Peru) "United Left (Peru)") party. However, Barrantes withdrew from the runoff, saying he did not want to prolong the country's political uncertainty. García was thus declared President on 1 June and took power on 28 July. For the first time in its 60-year history, the [APRA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Popular_Revolutionary_Alliance "American Popular Revolutionary Alliance") party came to power in Peru. Aged 36, García was dubbed "[Latin America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_America "Latin America")'s [Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy "John F. Kennedy")", becoming the region's youngest president at the time[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-britbio-20) and the second-youngest president in Peruvian history (the youngest was [Juan Crisostomo Torrico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Crisostomo_Torrico "Juan Crisostomo Torrico") in 1842, aged 34).

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/da/Felipe_Gonz%C3%A1lez_recibe_al_presidente_de_Per%C3%BA._Pool_Moncloa._30_de_enero_de_1987.jpeg/250px-Felipe_Gonz%C3%A1lez_recibe_al_presidente_de_Per%C3%BA._Pool_Moncloa._30_de_enero_de_1987.jpeg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Felipe_Gonz%C3%A1lez_recibe_al_presidente_de_Per%C3%BA._Pool_Moncloa._30_de_enero_de_1987.jpeg)

Alan García and Spanish Prime Minister [Felipe González](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felipe_Gonz%C3%A1lez "Felipe González") at [Moncloa Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palace_of_Moncloa "Palace of Moncloa"), January 1987.

His economic policy was based on APRA's initial anti-imperialist values. García distanced Peru from international markets, resulting in lower investment in the country.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-:1-5) Despite his initial popularity among voters, García's term in office was marked by bouts of [hyperinflation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperinflation "Hyperinflation"), which reached 7,649% in 1990[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-britbio-20) and had a cumulative total of 2,200,200% over five years, destabilizing the Peruvian economy. Foreign debt under García's administration increased to $19 billion by 1989.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-:1-5) Owing to this [chronic inflation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chronic_inflation "Chronic inflation"), the Peruvian currency, the [sol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peruvian_sol_(1863%E2%80%931985) "Peruvian sol (1863–1985)"), was replaced by the [inti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peruvian_inti "Peruvian inti") in February 1985 (before his presidency began), which itself was replaced by the [nuevo sol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peruvian_nuevo_sol "Peruvian nuevo sol") ("new sun") in July 1991, at which time the new sol had a cumulative value of one billion (1,000,000,000) old soles.

According to studies by the [National Institute of Statistics and Informatics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/INEI "INEI") and the [United Nations Development Programme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Development_Programme "United Nations Development Programme"),[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-25) around the start of his presidency, 41.6% of Peruvians lived in poverty. During his presidency, this increased to 55% in 1991. García also attempted to [nationalise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationalization "Nationalization") the banking and insurance industries. The [International Monetary Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Monetary_Fund "International Monetary Fund") and the financial community recoiled after García's administration unilaterally declared a limit on debt repayment equal to 10% of the [Gross National Product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gross_National_Product "Gross National Product"), thereby isolating Peru from international financial markets.

His presidency was marked by corruption and world-record hyperinflation, with the annual rate exceeding 13,000%. The administration devastated the local economy as well as all governmental institutions. Hunger, corruption, injustice, abuse of power, partisan elitism, and social unrest rose to dramatic levels throughout the nation due to García's misdeeds and incompetence, spurring terrorism. The economic turbulence exacerbated social tensions and contributed in great part to the rise of the violent [Maoist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maoist "Maoist") rebel movement known as the [Shining Path](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shining_Path "Shining Path"), which launched the [internal conflict in Peru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internal_conflict_in_Peru "Internal conflict in Peru") and began attacking electrical towers, causing a number of blackouts in Lima. The period also saw the emergence of the [Túpac Amaru Revolutionary Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%C3%BApac_Amaru_Revolutionary_Movement "Túpac Amaru Revolutionary Movement") (MRTA).[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-26) The García administration unsuccessfully sought a military solution to the growing terrorism, allegedly committing human rights violations, which are still under investigation. These include the [Accomarca massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accomarca_massacre "Accomarca massacre"), where 47 [campesinos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peasant "Peasant") were gunned down by armed forces in August 1985;[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-ipsnews-27) the [Cayara massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cayara_massacre "Cayara massacre") (May 1988), in which some 30 people were killed and dozens disappeared;[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-28) and [the summary execution of more than 200 inmates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peruvian_prison_massacres "Peruvian prison massacres") during prison riots in Lurigancho, San Juan Bautista ([El Frontón](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Front%C3%B3n "El Frontón")) and Santa Bárbara in 1986.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-29)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-HRW-30) According to an official inquiry, an estimated 1,600 [forced disappearances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forced_disappearance "Forced disappearance") took place during García's presidency. His own personal involvement in these events is not clear. García was allegedly[_[by whom?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Words\_to\_watch#Unsupported\_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")_] tied to the paramilitary [Rodrigo Franco Command](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodrigo_Franco_Command "Rodrigo Franco Command"), which is accused of carrying out political murders in Peru during his presidency. A U.S. [declassified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classified_information "Classified information") report, written in late 1987, said that APRA and top government officials were running a [paramilitary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramilitary "Paramilitary") group responsible for the attempted bombing of the _[El Diario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El\_Diario\_(Peru)?action=edit&redlink=1 "El Diario (Peru) (page does not exist)")_ newspaper, then linked to Shining Path, had sent people to train in [North Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Korea "North Korea"), and may have been involved in executions.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-Ko-31) According to investigative journalist [Lucy Komisar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucy_Komisar "Lucy Komisar"), the report made clear that García had given the orders.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-Ko-31)

García's historical economic failures were used by economists [Rudi Dornbusch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudi_Dornbusch "Rudi Dornbusch") and [Sebastian Edwards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sebastian_Edwards "Sebastian Edwards") to coin the term [macroeconomic populism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macroeconomic_populism "Macroeconomic populism").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-paper-32) Because of García's unpopularity by the end of his first term, at his farewell speech on 28 July 1990 he was booed by the entire opposition forces and almost prevented from speaking. The opposition forces slammed their folders in their desks to interrupt García. Some opposition members even left the congress. The event was televised.

Later that day, the board of the Chamber of Deputies requested the creation of a special committee to investigate García's presidency, accusing him of massive corruption and illicit enrichment. The committee attacked García with numerous proven accusations involving embezzlement, misappropriation and bribery, based on—among other sources—a U.S. congressional investigation that linked him to the [BCCI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_Credit_and_Commerce_International "Bank of Credit and Commerce International") scandal and had found millions of illicitly obtained dollars in BCCI as well as other banks.

In 1991, New York District Attorney [Robert Morgenthau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Morgenthau "Robert Morgenthau") charged García officially. Later in 1992, then-U.S. Senator [John Kerry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kerry "John Kerry") presided over the BCCI scandal report,[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-33) which concluded García was not only guilty of corruption but directly involved in an international racketeering network with activities that included drug and arms trafficking. Finally, the [Peruvian Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_Peru "Supreme Court of Peru") declared null all the probes and constitutional accusations gathered against García, allowing him to return to Peru after a 9-year self-imposed exile.

## Exile

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alan_Garc%C3%ADa&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Exile")]

On 5 April 1992, [Alberto Fujimori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alberto_Fujimori "Alberto Fujimori") conducted a [self-coup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_Peruvian_coup_d'%C3%A9tat "1992 Peruvian coup d'état"), whereby he dissolved the [Peruvian Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congress_of_the_Republic_of_Peru "Congress of the Republic of Peru") unconstitutionally and intervened in the Judiciary and other public institutions. Various politicians were persecuted and prevented from leaving their homes. García had been serving as [Senator for life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senator_for_life "Senator for life") since 1990, although he was unable to perform his duty due to the accusations of the Chamber of Deputies. On 18 October 1991, the Senate debated the proposal made by the lower house to indict García for crimes of illicit enrichment and against the public faith, allegedly committed when he was performing public functions. The Senate suspended García from the exercise of his functions as senator for life and put him on trial for alleged illicit enrichment during his presidential term with 38 votes in favor and 17 against.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-34) He was able to return to the Senate in March 1992, after the [Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_Peru "Supreme Court of Peru") dropped all constitutional charges against him. According to [Jorge Del Castillo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Del_Castillo "Jorge Del Castillo") in 2008, Fujimori ordered [Vladimiro Montesinos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimiro_Montesinos "Vladimiro Montesinos") to capture and assassinate García on the day of the coup.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-35)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-36) According to his own testimony, García escaped his home while military tanks took over the bloc where he lived.

After weeks of hiding in a construction site, he was able to enter the [residence of the Colombian Ambassador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_diplomatic_missions_of_Colombia "List of diplomatic missions of Colombia") at the end of May, where he requested political asylum.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-37) The request was granted on 1 June by the government of President [César Gaviria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A9sar_Gaviria "César Gaviria"). García left Peru through a pass that allowed him to board a [Colombian Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombian_Air_Force "Colombian Air Force") jet that transferred him to [Bogotá](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bogot%C3%A1 "Bogotá"), along with then congressman [Jorge Del Castillo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Del_Castillo "Jorge Del Castillo"). García arrived at Catam military airport and in statements to the press promised to fight Fujimori's dictatorship.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-38) The regime opened judicial processes to investigate illicit enrichment and accusations of corruption; after that, García's extradition was requested from the Colombian government, but was denied.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-39)

In 1994, the Human Rights Commission of the [Organization of American States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organization_of_American_States "Organization of American States") denounced the Fujimori government for violation of the rights to liberty, security and due defense of García and asked the Peruvian government to nullify the processes initiated.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-40)

In April 1995, Congress lifted García's parliamentary immunity in response to accusations that he had taken bribes from the Italian consortium Tralima for the construction of the [Lima Metro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lima_Metro "Lima Metro"). Based on this, the Civil Sector of the [Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_Peru "Supreme Court of Peru") again requested García's extradition from Colombia, which was denied because García went to live in [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris") for the rest of his exile.

Between 1993 and 2001, García did not actively participate in Peruvian politics, except in the publication of some works on his first presidency, and a literary work, _El Mundo de Maquiavelo_ (_The World of [Machiavelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niccol%C3%B2\_Machiavelli "Niccolò Machiavelli")_). He continued denouncing the human rights violations committed by the Fujimori administration. On rare occasions, he appeared on Peruvian television and radio from Bogotá.

In 2001, the Supreme Court declared the allegations that were imputed to him at the end of his first term had been annulled.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-41)

## Return to politics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alan_Garc%C3%ADa&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Return to politics")]

### 2001 Peruvian national election

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alan_Garc%C3%ADa&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 2001 Peruvian national election")]

Alan García returned to Lima on January 27, 2001, at 5:35pm. His return caused so much anticipation that a huge crowd of supporters was waiting for him at the airport chanting his name and showing support with hundreds of signs with the words "ALAN VUELVE". That same day at 8:30pm a rally was called in the Plaza San Martin de Lima where Garcia gave a speech in front of a large crowd.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-42) Some say[_[who?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Words\_to\_watch#Unsupported\_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")_] there were around 20,000 people that night. Garcia ran for president in the new elections called by the interim president [Valentín Paniagua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valent%C3%ADn_Paniagua "Valentín Paniagua"), and in a 60-day election campaign he finished in second place in the first round behind [Alejandro Toledo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alejandro_Toledo "Alejandro Toledo"), qualifying him for the second round. Toledo's popularity remained stable, while Garcia's popularity was based on his innovative proposals on the issue of the agrarian bank,[_[further explanation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_] not continuing with a [neoliberal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoliberal "Neoliberal") model, etc. However, it was not enough to acquire more endorsements and support from Peruvian voters and Alejandro Toledo won the general elections in the second round with 53.1% of the vote against Garcia's 46.9%. After the [2001 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Peruvian_general_election "2001 Peruvian general election"), Garcia, as leader of the APRA party, became Leader of the Opposition.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garc%C3%ADa#cite_note-britbio-20)

### 2006 Peruvian national election

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Alan_Garc%C3%ADa&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 2006 Peruvian national election")]
