**María Corazón** "**Cory**" **Sumulong Cojuangco-Aquino**[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-nhcp-1)[CCLH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Legion_of_Honor "Philippine Legion of Honor") (Tagalog:[[kɔɾaˈsɔn kɔˈhwaŋkɔ aˈkino]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Tagalog "Help:IPA/Tagalog"); January 25, 1933 – August 1, 2009) was a Filipino politician who served as the 11th [president of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Philippines "President of the Philippines"), serving from 1986 to 1992. The [first female president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_elected_and_appointed_female_heads_of_state_and_government "List of elected and appointed female heads of state and government") in Philippine history, Aquino was the most prominent figure of the 1986 [People Power Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People_Power_Revolution "People Power Revolution"), which ended the [two-decade rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Philippines_(1965%E2%80%931986) "History of the Philippines (1965–1986)") of President [Ferdinand Marcos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos "Ferdinand Marcos") and led to the establishment of the current democratic [Fifth Philippine Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Philippines_(1986%E2%80%93present) "History of the Philippines (1986–present)"). She has been regarded by media outlets as the "Mother of [Democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democracy "Democracy")".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-5)

Aquino was married to Senator [Benigno Aquino Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benigno_Aquino_Jr. "Benigno Aquino Jr."), a prominent critic of President Marcos. The couple had five children, including 15th president [Benigno Aquino III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benigno_Aquino_III "Benigno Aquino III") and entertainer [Kris Aquino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kris_Aquino "Kris Aquino"). After the [assassination of her husband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Benigno_Aquino_Jr. "Assassination of Benigno Aquino Jr.") on August 21, 1983, she emerged as leader of the opposition against the president. In late 1985, Marcos called for a [snap election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snap_election "Snap election"), and Aquino ran for president with former Senator [Salvador Laurel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvador_Laurel "Salvador Laurel") as her running mate for [vice president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_Philippines "Vice President of the Philippines"). After the [February 7, 1986, presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1986_Philippine_presidential_election "1986 Philippine presidential election"), the [Batasang Pambansa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batasang_Pambansa "Batasang Pambansa") proclaimed Marcos and his running mate [Arturo Tolentino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arturo_Tolentino "Arturo Tolentino") as the winners, which prompted allegations of [electoral fraud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_fraud "Electoral fraud") and Aquino's call for massive [civil disobedience](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_disobedience "Civil disobedience") actions.

Subsequently, the People Power Revolution, a [non-violent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonviolent_revolution "Nonviolent revolution")[mass demonstration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demonstration_(political) "Demonstration (political)") movement, took place from February 22 to 25. With support from the [Philippine Catholic Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church_in_the_Philippines "Catholic Church in the Philippines") and defections from the [Armed Forces of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armed_Forces_of_the_Philippines "Armed Forces of the Philippines"), the People Power Revolution ousted Marcos, and Aquino, with no prior political experience, was sworn in to the presidency on February 25, 1986.

As president, Aquino spearheaded the development of the [1987 Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_the_Philippines "Constitution of the Philippines"), which limited the powers of the presidency and re-established the [bicameral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicameral "Bicameral")[Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congress_of_the_Philippines "Congress of the Philippines"), removing the previous dictatorial government structure. The constitution also affirmed social justice and equality as guiding principles of national development, reinforcing efforts to promote civil liberties, democratic participation, and social cohesion following the end of authoritarian rule.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-6) Her economic policies focused on forging good economic standing amongst the international community as well as disestablishing Marcos-era [crony capitalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crony_capitalist "Crony capitalist") monopolies, emphasizing the [free market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_market "Free market") and responsible economy. Her administration pursued peace talks to resolve the [Moro conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moro_conflict "Moro conflict"), and the result of these talks was creation of the [Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autonomous_Region_in_Muslim_Mindanao "Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao").

Aquino was criticized for the [Mendiola Massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mendiola_Massacre "Mendiola Massacre"), which resulted in the shooting deaths of at least 12 peaceful protesters by Philippine state security forces. The Philippines faced various natural calamities in the latter part of Aquino's administration, such as the [1990 Luzon earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990_Luzon_earthquake "1990 Luzon earthquake"), [1991 Mt. Pinatubo eruption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991_eruption_of_Mount_Pinatubo "1991 eruption of Mount Pinatubo") and [Tropical Storm Thelma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_Storm_Thelma "Tropical Storm Thelma"). [Several coup attempts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coup_attempts_against_Corazon_Aquino "Coup attempts against Corazon Aquino") were made against her government. She left office in 1992 and remained active in political activities. Aquino was diagnosed with [colorectal cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorectal_cancer "Colorectal cancer") in 2008 and [died](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_and_funeral_of_Corazon_Aquino "Death and funeral of Corazon Aquino") the following year. Her funeral was the subject of global media coverage, and monuments and public landmarks in the country were named in her honor.

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Corazon_Aquino&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Cory Aquino was born as María Corazón Sumulong Cojuangco on January 25, 1933, in [Paniqui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paniqui,_Tarlac "Paniqui, Tarlac"), Tarlac.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-malacanang.gov.ph-7) She was born to the prominent [Cojuangco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cojuangco "Cojuangco") family. Her father was [José Cojuangco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Cojuangco "José Cojuangco"), a prominent Tarlac businessman and former congressman, and her mother was Demetria Sumulong, a pharmacist. Both of Aquino's parents were from prominent political families. Aquino's grandfather from her father's side, Melecio Cojuangco, was a member of the historic [Malolos Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malolos_Congress "Malolos Congress"), and Aquino's mother belonged to the politically influential Sumulong family of [Rizal province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rizal_province "Rizal province"), which included [Juan Sumulong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Sumulong "Juan Sumulong"), who ran against [Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_the_Philippines "Commonwealth of the Philippines") President [Manuel L. Quezon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_L._Quezon "Manuel L. Quezon") in 1941 and Senator [Lorenzo Sumulong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorenzo_Sumulong "Lorenzo Sumulong"), who was later appointed by Aquino in the [Constitutional Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Constitutional_Commission_of_1986 "Philippine Constitutional Commission of 1986"). Aquino was the sixth of eight children, two of whom died in infancy. Her siblings were Pedro, Josephine, Teresita, Jose Jr., and Maria Paz.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-Corazon-8)

Aquino spent her elementary school days at [St. Scholastica's College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Scholastica's_College_Manila "St. Scholastica's College Manila") in Manila, where she graduated at the top of her class as valedictorian. She transferred to [Assumption Convent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assumption_College_San_Lorenzo "Assumption College San Lorenzo"), then also in Manila, to pursue high school studies. After her family moved to the United States, she attended the Assumption-run [Ravenhill Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ravenhill_Academy "Ravenhill Academy") in [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia"). She then transferred to [Notre Dame Convent School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Notre_Dame_School_(Manhattan) "Notre Dame School (Manhattan)") in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), where she graduated from in 1949. During her high school years in the United States, Aquino volunteered for the campaign of U.S. [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_in_the_United_States "Republican Party in the United States") presidential candidate [Thomas Dewey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Dewey "Thomas Dewey") against [Democratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") incumbent [U.S. President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States")[Harry S. Truman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman "Harry S. Truman") during the [1948 United States presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1948_United_States_presidential_election "1948 United States presidential election").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-Corazon-8) After graduating from high school, she pursued her college education at the [College of Mount Saint Vincent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_Mount_Saint_Vincent "College of Mount Saint Vincent") in New York, graduating in 1953 with a major in French and minor in mathematics.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-9)

## Wife of Benigno Aquino Jr.

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Corazon_Aquino&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Wife of Benigno Aquino Jr.")]

After graduating from college, she returned to the Philippines and studied law at [Far Eastern University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far_Eastern_University "Far Eastern University") in 1953.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-9facts-10) While attending, she met [Benigno "Ninoy" S. Aquino Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benigno_Aquino_Jr. "Benigno Aquino Jr."), who was the son of the late Speaker [Benigno S. Aquino Sr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benigno_Aquino_Sr. "Benigno Aquino Sr.") and a grandson of General [Servillano Aquino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Servillano_Aquino "Servillano Aquino"). She discontinued her law education and married Benigno at the [Our Lady of Sorrows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Our_Lady_of_Sorrows "Our Lady of Sorrows") Parish in [Pasay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasay "Pasay"), [Rizal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rizal_(province) "Rizal (province)") on October 11, 1954.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-11) The couple had five children: Maria Elena ("Ballsy"; born 1955), Aurora Corazon ("Pinky"; born 1957), [Benigno Simeon III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benigno_Aquino_III "Benigno Aquino III") ("Noynoy"; 1960–2021), Victoria Elisa ("Viel"; born 1961) and [Kristina Bernadette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kris_Aquino "Kris Aquino") ("Kris"; born 1971).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-cory1-13)

Aquino initially had difficulty adjusting to provincial life when she and her husband moved to [Concepcion, Tarlac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concepcion,_Tarlac "Concepcion, Tarlac") in 1955. Aquino found herself bored in Concepcion, and welcomed the opportunity to have dinner with her husband inside the [American military facility at nearby Clark Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clark_Air_Base "Clark Air Base").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-lt-14) Afterwards, the Aquino family moved to a bungalow in suburban [Quezon City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quezon_City "Quezon City").

Throughout her life, Aquino was known to be a devout [Roman Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church_in_the_Philippines "Catholic Church in the Philippines").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-9facts-10)

Corazon Aquino was fluent in [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"), [Japanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_language "Japanese language"), [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"), and [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language "English language") aside from her native [Tagalog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tagalog_language "Tagalog language") and [Kapampangan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kapampangan_language "Kapampangan language").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-9facts-10)

Ninoy Aquino, a former [Nacionalista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nacionalista_Party "Nacionalista Party") turned [Liberal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Party_(Philippines) "Liberal Party (Philippines)"), rose to become the youngest governor in the country in 1961 and then the youngest senator ever elected to the [Senate of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_of_the_Philippines "Senate of the Philippines") in [1967](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1967_Philippine_Senate_election "1967 Philippine Senate election"). For most of her husband's political career, Aquino remained a housewife who raised their children and hosted her spouse's political allies who would visit their Quezon City home.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-pi-15) She would decline to join her husband on stage during campaign rallies, instead preferring to be in the back of the audience and listen to him.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-lt-14) Unbeknownst to many at the time, Corazon Aquino sold some of her prized inheritance to fund the candidacy of her husband.

As Ninoy emerged as a leading critic of the government of [President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Philippines "President of the Philippines")[Ferdinand Marcos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos "Ferdinand Marcos"), he became seen as a strong candidate for president to succeed Marcos in the 1973 elections. However, Marcos, who was barred by the [1935 Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_the_Philippines#1935_Constitution "Constitution of the Philippines") to seek a third term, [declared martial law on September 21, 1972](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martial_law_under_Ferdinand_Marcos "Martial law under Ferdinand Marcos") and later abolished the constitution, thereby allowing him to remain in office. Ninoy Aquino was among the first to be arrested at the onset of martial law, and was later sentenced to death. During her husband's incarceration, Corazon Aquino stopped going to beauty salons or buying new clothes and prohibited her children from attending parties, until a priest advised her and her children to try to live as normal lives as possible.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-lt-14)

Despite Corazon's initial opposition, Ninoy decided to run in the [1978 Batasang Pambansa elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1978_Philippine_parliamentary_election "1978 Philippine parliamentary election") from his prison cell as party leader of the newly created [LABAN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lakas_ng_Bayan "Lakas ng Bayan"). Corazon Aquino campaigned on behalf of her husband and delivered a political speech for the first time in her life during this political campaign. In 1980 Ninoy suffered a heart attack, and Marcos allowed Senator Aquino and his family to leave for exile in the United States upon intervention from U.S. president [Jimmy Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter "Jimmy Carter") so that Aquino could seek medical treatment.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-fb-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-campaign-17)

On August 21, 1983, Ninoy ended his stay in the United States and returned without his family to the Philippines, where he was [immediately assassinated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Benigno_Aquino_Jr. "Assassination of Benigno Aquino Jr.") on a staircase leading to the tarmac of [Manila International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ninoy_Aquino_International_Airport "Ninoy Aquino International Airport"). The airport is now named Ninoy Aquino International Airport, renamed by the [Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congress_of_the_Philippines "Congress of the Philippines") in his honor in 1987. Corazon Aquino returned to the Philippines a few days later and led her husband's funeral procession, in which more than two million people participated.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-fb-16)

## 1986 presidential campaign

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Corazon_Aquino&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1986 presidential campaign")]

Main article: [1986 Philippine presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1986_Philippine_presidential_election "1986 Philippine presidential election")

Following her husband's assassination in 1983, Corazon Aquino became active in various demonstrations held against the Marcos regime. She began to assume the mantle of leadership left by her husband and became a figurehead of the anti-Marcos political opposition. On November 3, 1985, during an interview with American journalist [David Brinkley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Brinkley "David Brinkley") on _[This Week with David Brinkley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/This\_Week\_with\_David\_Brinkley "This Week with David Brinkley")_, Marcos suddenly announced [snap elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snap_election "Snap election") that would be held within three months to dispel doubt against his regime's legitimate authority, an action that surprised the nation.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-18) The election was later scheduled to be held on February 7, 1986. A petition was organized to urge Aquino to run for president, headed by former newspaper publisher [Joaquin Roces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chino_Roces "Chino Roces").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-19) On December 1, the petition of 1.2 million signatures was publicly presented to Aquino in an event attended by 15,000 people, and on December 3, Aquino officially declared her candidacy.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-20)[United Opposition (UNIDO)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nationalist_Democratic_Organization "United Nationalist Democratic Organization") party leader [Salvador Laurel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvador_Laurel "Salvador Laurel") was chosen as Aquino's running mate as candidate for vice president.

During the campaign, Marcos attacked Corazon Aquino on her husband's previous ties to [communists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Communist_Party "Philippine Communist Party"),[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-21) characterizing the election as a fight "between democracy and communism".[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-22) Aquino refuted Marcos' charge and stated that she would not appoint a single communist to her cabinet.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-23) Marcos also accused Aquino of playing "[political football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_football "Political football")" with the United States in regards to the continued United States military presence in the Philippines at [Clark Air Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clark_Air_Base "Clark Air Base") and [Subic Naval Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subic_Naval_Base "Subic Naval Base").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-24) Another point of attack for Marcos was Aquino's inexperience in public office. Marcos' campaign was characterized by [sexist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexist "Sexist") attacks, such as remarks by Marcos that Aquino was "just a woman" and that a woman's remarks should be limited to the bedroom.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-25)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-fb-16)

The [snap election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1986_Philippine_presidential_election "1986 Philippine presidential election") was held on February 7, 1986, and was marred by massive electoral fraud, violence, intimidation, coercion, and disenfranchisement of voters. On February 11, while votes were still being tabulated, former [Antique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antique_(province) "Antique (province)") Governor [Evelio Javier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evelio_Javier "Evelio Javier"), who had been director of Aquino's campaign in Antique, was assassinated. During the tallying of votes conducted by the [Commission on Elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commission_on_Elections "Commission on Elections") (COMELEC), 30 poll computer technicians walked out to contest the alleged election-rigging being done in favor of Marcos. Years later it was claimed that the walkout of computer technicians was led by Linda Kapunan,[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-26) wife of Lt Col Eduardo Kapunan, a leader of [Reform the Armed Forces Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_the_Armed_Forces_Movement "Reform the Armed Forces Movement") that plotted to attack the [Malacañang Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaca%C3%B1ang_Palace "Malacañang Palace") and kill Marcos and his family, leading to a partial reevaluation of the walkout event.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-Manila_Times-28)

On February 15, 1986, the [Batasang Pambansa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batasang_Pambansa "Batasang Pambansa"), which was dominated by Marcos' ruling party and its allies, declared President Marcos as the winner of the election. However, [NAMFREL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Citizens'_Movement_for_Free_Elections "National Citizens' Movement for Free Elections")'s electoral count showed that Corazon Aquino had won. Aquino claimed victory according to NAMFREL's electoral count and called for a rally dubbed "Tagumpay ng Bayan" (People's Victory Rally) the following day to protest the declaration by the Batasang Pambansa.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-29) Aquino also called for boycotts against products and services from companies controlled or owned by individuals closely allied with Marcos. The rally was held at the historic [Rizal Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rizal_Park "Rizal Park") in Luneta, Manila and drew a pro-Aquino crowd of around two million people. The dubious election results drew condemnation from both domestic and foreign powers. The [Catholic Bishops' Conference of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Bishops'_Conference_of_the_Philippines "Catholic Bishops' Conference of the Philippines") issued a statement strongly criticizing the conduct of the election, describing the election as violent and fraudulent. The [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") likewise condemned the election.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-pi-15)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-bbc-30) Aquino rejected a power-sharing agreement proposed by the American diplomat [Philip Habib](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Habib "Philip Habib"), who had been sent as an emissary by U.S. President [Ronald Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan "Ronald Reagan") to help defuse the tension.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-bbc-30)

### Accession as president

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Corazon_Aquino&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Accession as president")]

Main article: [People Power Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People_Power_Revolution "People Power Revolution")

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b9/Corazon_Aquino_inauguration.jpg/330px-Corazon_Aquino_inauguration.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Corazon_Aquino_inauguration.jpg)

Aquino takes the oath of office before [Chief Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_Justice_of_the_Philippines "Chief Justice of the Philippines")[Claudio Teehankee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claudio_Teehankee "Claudio Teehankee") Sr. in [Club Filipino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_Filipino "Club Filipino"), [San Juan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Juan,_Metro_Manila "San Juan, Metro Manila") on February 25, 1986

On February 22, 1986, disgruntled and reformist military officers led by Defense Minister [Juan Ponce Enrile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Ponce_Enrile "Juan Ponce Enrile") and General [Fidel V. Ramos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fidel_V._Ramos "Fidel V. Ramos") surprised the nation and the international community by the announcement of their defection from the Marcos government, citing a strong belief that Aquino was the real winner in the contested presidential election. Enrile, Ramos, and the rebel soldiers then set up operations in [Camp Aguinaldo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camp_Aguinaldo "Camp Aguinaldo"), the headquarters of the [Armed Forces of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armed_Forces_of_the_Philippines "Armed Forces of the Philippines"), and [Camp Crame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camp_Crame "Camp Crame"), the headquarters of the [Philippine Constabulary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Constabulary "Philippine Constabulary"), across [Epifanio de los Santos Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epifanio_de_los_Santos_Avenue "Epifanio de los Santos Avenue") (EDSA). Cardinal Sin appealed to the public in a broadcast over Church-run [Radyo Veritas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DZRV-AM "DZRV-AM"), and millions of Filipinos gathered to the part of [Epifanio De Los Santos Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EDSA "EDSA") between the two camps to give their support and prayers to the rebels.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-31) At that time, Aquino was meditating in a [Carmelite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmelite "Carmelite") convent in [Cebu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cebu "Cebu"). Upon learning of the defection, Aquino and Cardinal Sin appeared on Radyo Veritas to rally behind Enrile and Ramos. Aquino then flew back to Manila to prepare for the takeover of the government.

Aquino was sworn in as the eleventh president of the Philippines on February 25, 1986. An hour after Aquino's inauguration, Marcos held his own inauguration ceremony at the Malacañang Palace. Later that same day, Ferdinand E. Marcos fled from the Philippines to [Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii "Hawaii").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-32)

## Presidency (1986–1992)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Corazon_Aquino&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Presidency (1986–1992)")]

Main article: [Presidency of Corazon Aquino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Corazon_Aquino "Presidency of Corazon Aquino")

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e4/Cory_Aquino_during_a_ceremony_honoring_US_Air_Force.jpg/250px-Cory_Aquino_during_a_ceremony_honoring_US_Air_Force.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cory_Aquino_during_a_ceremony_honoring_US_Air_Force.jpg)

Aquino during a ceremony honoring the United States Air Force

Corazon Aquino's accession to the presidency marked the end of authoritarian rule in the Philippines. Aquino is the first female president of the Philippines and is still the only president of the Philippines to have never held any prior political position. Aquino is regarded as the first [female president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_elected_and_appointed_female_heads_of_state "List of elected and appointed female heads of state") in [Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia "Asia").

### Transitional government and creation of new constitution

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Corazon_Aquino&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Transitional government and creation of new constitution")]

On February 25, 1986, the first day of her administration, Aquino issued Proclamation No. 1, which announced an intention to reorganize the government and called on all officials appointed by Marcos to resign, starting with members of the [Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_Philippines "Supreme Court of the Philippines").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-33) On March 25, 1986, President Aquino issued [Proclamation No. 3](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Constitution%20of%20the%20Philippines%20(1973)#1986_Amendment_(Proclamation_No._3_and_the_1986_Provisional_Constitution) "s:Constitution of the Philippines (1973)"), which announced a transitional government into a democratic system. She abolished the [1973 Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sb._1973 "Sb. 1973") that was in force during the [martial law era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martial_Law_under_Ferdinand_Marcos "Martial Law under Ferdinand Marcos"), and by decree issued the [provisional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provisional_constitution "Provisional constitution")[1986 Freedom Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_the_Philippines#%22Freedom_Constitution%22_(1986) "Constitution of the Philippines"), pending the ratification of a more formal and comprehensive charter. This constitutional allowed her to exercise both executive and legislative powers during the period of transitional government.

After the issuance of Proclamation No. 1, all 15 members of the Supreme Court submitted their resignations.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-34) Aquino then reorganized the membership of the Supreme Court with the stated purpose of restoring its [judicial independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judicial_independence "Judicial independence"). On May 22, 1986, in the case _Lawyers League v. President Aquino_, the reorganized Supreme Court declared the Aquino government as "not merely a _[de facto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De\_facto "De facto")_ government but in fact and law a _[de jure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De\_jure "De jure")_ government", and affirmed its legitimacy.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-35)

Aquino appointed all 48 members of the [1986 Constitutional Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Constitutional_Commission_of_1986 "Philippine Constitutional Commission of 1986") ("Con-Com"), led by retired activist and former Supreme Court Associate Justice [Cecilia Muñoz-Palma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecilia_Mu%C3%B1oz-Palma "Cecilia Muñoz-Palma"), which was tasked with writing a new constitution. The Commission completed its final draft of the Constitution in October 1986.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-36)

On February 2, 1987, the [Constitution of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_the_Philippines "Constitution of the Philippines") was ratified by [nationwide plebiscite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1987_Philippine_constitutional_plebiscite "1987 Philippine constitutional plebiscite"). It remains the [constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution "Constitution") of the Philippines to the present day. The Constitution established a [bill of rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_of_rights "Bill of rights") and a three-branch government consisting of the executive department, the legislative department, and the judicial department. The Constitution restored the [bicameral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicameralism "Bicameralism") Congress, which in 1973 had been abolished by Marcos and replaced with first the [Batasang Bayan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batasang_Bayan "Batasang Bayan") and later the Batasang Pambansa.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-37) The ratification of the new Constitution was soon followed by the [election of senators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1987_Philippine_Senate_election "1987 Philippine Senate election") and the [election of House of Representatives members](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1987_Philippine_House_of_Representatives_elections "1987 Philippine House of Representatives elections") on May 11, 1987, as well as [local elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1988_Philippine_local_elections "1988 Philippine local elections") on January 18, 1988.

### Legal reforms

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Corazon_Aquino&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Legal reforms")]

After the ratification of the constitution, Aquino promulgated two landmark [legal codes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_legal_codes "Philippine legal codes"), namely, the [Family Code of 1987](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_Code_of_the_Philippines "Family Code of the Philippines"), which reformed the [civil law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_law_(legal_system) "Civil law (legal system)") on family relations, and the [Administrative Code of 1987](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_legal_codes#Philippine_legal_codes "Philippine legal codes"), which reorganized the structure of the [executive department of government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Departments_of_the_Philippines "Executive Departments of the Philippines"). Another landmark law that was enacted during her tenure was the 1991 [Local Government Code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_Government_Code "Local Government Code"), which devolved national government powers to local government units (LGUs). The new Code enhanced the power of LGUs to enact local taxation measures and assured them of a share in the national revenue.

During Aquino's tenure, vital economic laws such as the Built-Operate-Transfer Law, Foreign Investments Act, and the Consumer Protection and Welfare Act were also enacted.

Although [capital punishment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_punishment "Capital punishment") was [abolished](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_punishment_in_the_Philippines "Capital punishment in the Philippines") by the 1987 Constitution, President Aquino later pushed for its reinstatement by 1989, and was further convinced in her stance by early 1990 after the deaths of two young rape victims in Pangasinan.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-40)

The economy posted a positive growth of 3.4% during Aquino's first year in office, and continued to grow at an overall positive rate throughout her tenure for an average rate of 3.4% from 1986 to 1992. Real GDP growth suffered a 0.4% decrease in 1991 in the aftermath of the [1989 coup attempt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_Philippine_coup_attempt "1989 Philippine coup attempt") by the Reform the Armed Forces Movement, which shook international confidence in the Philippine economy and hindered foreign investment.

Aquino made fighting inflation one of her priorities after the nation suffered from skyrocketing prices during the last years of the Marcos administration. The last six years of the Marcos administration recorded an average annual inflation rate of 20.9%, which peaked in 1984 at 50.3%. From 1986 to 1992, the Philippines recorded an average annual inflation rate of 9.2%. During the Aquino administration, the annual inflation rate peaked at 18.1% in 1991; a stated reason for this increase was [panic buying](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panic_buying "Panic buying") during the [Gulf War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_War "Gulf War").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-45) Overall, the economy under Aquino had an average growth of 3.8% from 1986 to 1992.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-46)

#### De-monopolization

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Corazon_Aquino&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: De-monopolization")]

One of Aquino's first actions as president was to seize Marcos' multi-billion dollar [fortune of ill-gotten wealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#Ill-gotten_wealth_and_kleptocracy "Ferdinand Marcos"). On February 28, 1986, four days into her presidency, Aquino formed the [Presidential Commission on Good Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_Commission_on_Good_Government "Presidential Commission on Good Government") (PCGG), which was tasked with retrieving Marcos' domestic and international fortune.

After his declaration of martial law in 1972 and his consolidation of authoritarian power, President Ferdinand Marcos issued various government decrees that awarded [monopoly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monopoly "Monopoly") or [oligopoly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oligopoly "Oligopoly") power over entire industries to various [close associates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cronies_of_Ferdinand_Marcos "Cronies of Ferdinand Marcos"), in a scheme later regarded as [crony capitalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crony_capitalism "Crony capitalism"). President Aquino pursued a [market liberalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_market "Free market") agenda to combat this problem. President Aquino particularly targeted the [sugar industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugar_industry_of_the_Philippines "Sugar industry of the Philippines") and the [coconut industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coconut_production_in_the_Philippines "Coconut production in the Philippines") for de-monopolization.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-47)

#### Debt

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Corazon_Aquino&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Debt")]

[![Image 27](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1a/Vice_President_Dan_Quayle_and_President_Corizon_Aquino_of_the_Philippines_participate_in_the_Veterans%27_Day_Service_at_Arlington_National_Cemetery%2C_10_Nov_89.jpg/250px-Vice_President_Dan_Quayle_and_President_Corizon_Aquino_of_the_Philippines_participate_in_the_Veterans%27_Day_Service_at_Arlington_National_Cemetery%2C_10_Nov_89.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Vice_President_Dan_Quayle_and_President_Corizon_Aquino_of_the_Philippines_participate_in_the_Veterans'_Day_Service_at_Arlington_National_Cemetery,_10_Nov_89.jpg)

Aquino with U.S. Vice President [Dan Quayle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Quayle "Dan Quayle") participate in the Veterans' Day Service at [Arlington National Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlington_National_Cemetery "Arlington National Cemetery") on November 10, 1989.

Throughout the tenure of President Ferdinand Marcos, government [foreign debt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/External_debt "External debt") had ballooned from less than $3 billion in 1970 to $28 billion by the end of his administration, through [privatization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privatization "Privatization") of bad government assets and [deregulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deregulation "Deregulation") of many vital industries. The debt had badly tarnished the international credit standing and economic reputation of the country.

President Aquino inherited the debt of the Marcos administration and weighed all options on what to do with the debt, including not paying the debt. Aquino eventually chose to honor all the debts that were previously incurred in order to clear the country's economic reputation. Her decision proved to be unpopular but Aquino defended it, saying that was the most practical move. Beginning in 1986, the Aquino administration paid off $4 billion of the country's outstanding debts to improve its international credit ratings and attract the attention of foreign investors. This move also ensured lower interest rates and longer payment terms for future loans. During the Aquino administration, the Philippines acquired an additional $9 billion debt, increasing the net national debt by $5 billion within six years due to the need to infuse capital and money into the economy.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-48) The Aquino administration was able to reduce the Philippines' external [debt-to-GDP ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debt-to-GDP_ratio "Debt-to-GDP ratio") by 20.1 percent, from 87.9 percent at the start of the administration to 67.8 percent in 1991.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-49)

#### Agrarian reform

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Corazon_Aquino&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Agrarian reform")]

See also: [Land reform in the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_reform_in_the_Philippines "Land reform in the Philippines")

[![Image 28](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/President_Aquino_at_IRRI.jpg/250px-President_Aquino_at_IRRI.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:President_Aquino_at_IRRI.jpg)

Aquino holds talks with the officials from the [International Rice Research Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Rice_Research_Institute "International Rice Research Institute") in [Los Baños](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Ba%C3%B1os,_Laguna "Los Baños, Laguna"), [Laguna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laguna_(province) "Laguna (province)").

President Aquino envisioned agrarian and land reform as the centerpiece of her administration's social legislative agenda. However, her family background and social class as a privileged daughter of a wealthy and landed clan became a lightning rod of criticisms against her land reform agenda.

After the Mendiola Massacre and in response to calls for agrarian reform, President Aquino issued Presidential Proclamation 131 and Executive Order 229 on July 22, 1987, which outlined her land reform program, including sugar lands. In 1988, with the backing of Aquino, the new Congress of the Philippines passed Republic Act No. 6657, more popularly known as the "Comprehensive Agrarian Reform Law" (CARP), which paved the way for the redistribution of agricultural lands from landowners to tenant-farmers. Landowners were paid in exchange by the government through [just compensation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Just_compensation "Just compensation"), and were also not allowed to retain more than five hectares of land.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-RA6657-50):Section 6 The law also allowed corporate landowners to "voluntarily divest a proportion of their [capital stock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stock "Stock"), equity or participation in favor of their workers or other qualified beneficiaries", in lieu of turning over their land to the government for redistribution.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-RA6657-50):Section 31 Despite the flaws in the law, the Supreme Court upheld its constitutionality in 1989, declaring that the implementation of CARP was "a revolutionary kind of expropriation".[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-51)

Corazon Aquino herself was subject to a controversy that centered on [Hacienda Luisita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hacienda_Luisita "Hacienda Luisita"), a 6,453-hectare estate located in the province of Tarlac which she and her siblings inherited from her father José Cojuangco. Instead of land distribution, Hacienda Luisita reorganized itself into a corporation and distributed stock. As such, ownership of agricultural portions of the hacienda was transferred to the corporation, which in turn, gave its shares of stocks to farmers. Critics argued that Aquino bowed to pressure from relatives by allowing stock redistribution in lieu of land redistribution under CARP.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-pdihl-52)

The stock redistribution scheme was revoked in 2006, when the [Department of Agrarian Reform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Agrarian_Reform "Department of Agrarian Reform") ordered the mandatory redistribution of land to tenant-farmers of Hacienda Luisita. The Department of Agrarian Reform had looked into its revocation since 2004, when violence erupted in the hacienda over the retrenchment of workers, leaving seven people dead.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-pdihl-52)

### Coup attempts on Aquino government

From 1986 to 1990 numerous [coup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coup_d'%C3%A9tat "Coup d'état") attempts were enacted on the Aquino administration and the new Philippine government. Many of these attempts were conducted by the Reform the Armed Forces Movement, who attempted to establish a [military government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_government "Military government"), while other attempts were conducted by loyalists to former President Marcos.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

From 1986 to 1987 there were six plots to overthrow the Aquino government, with the deadliest being the August 1987 attempt which left 53 dead. The most serious attempt was staged in December 1989, following which President Aquino established a fact-finding commission headed by then-COMELEC Chairman Hilario Davide Jr.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-53)

### Mendiola massacre and cabinet infighting

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Corazon_Aquino&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Mendiola massacre and cabinet infighting")]

Main article: [Mendiola Massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mendiola_Massacre "Mendiola Massacre")

On January 22, 1987, during the era of transition government and shortly before the nationwide plebiscite to ratify the Constitution, 12 citizens were killed and 51 were injured in the [Mendiola Massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mendiola_Massacre "Mendiola Massacre"). The incident was initially a peaceful protest by agrarian workers and farmers who had marched to the historic Mendiola Street near the [Malacañan Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaca%C3%B1an_Palace "Malacañan Palace") to demand genuine land reform. The massacre occurred when Marines fired at farmers who tried to go beyond the designated demarcation line set by the police.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-54) The massacre resulted in several resignations from Aquino's cabinet, including [Jose W. Diokno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jose_W._Diokno "Jose W. Diokno"), head of the Presidential Committee on Human Rights, chairman of the [Commission on Human Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commission_on_Human_Rights "Commission on Human Rights") (CHR), and chairman of the government panel in charge of negotiations with rebel forces resigned from his government posts. His daughter Maris said, "It was the only time we saw him near tears."[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-dalisaybio-55)

In September 1987, Vice President Doy Laurel resigned as secretary of foreign affairs. In his resignation letter to Aquino, Laurel stated, "the past years of Marcos are now beginning to look no worse than your first two years in office. And the reported controversies and scandals involving your closest relatives have become the object of our people's outrage. From 16,500 NPA regular when Marcos fell, the communists now claim an armed strength of 25,200. From city to countryside, anarchy has spread. There is anarchy within the government, anarchy within the ruling coalesced parties and anarchy in the streets."[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-56)

Finance Minister [Jaime Ongpin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaime_Ongpin "Jaime Ongpin"), who had successfully advocated for paying external debt incurred during Marcos' administration, was dismissed by Aquino in September 1987 and later died in an apparent suicide in December 1987.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-57) His widow stated that he had been depressed due to infighting in Aquino's cabinet and lack of significant change since the People Power Revolution.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-58)

Soon after the Mendiola Massacre, the Aquino administration and Congress worked to pass significant agrarian reform, which culminated in the passage of the Comprehensive Agrarian Reform Law (CARP).

### Peace talks with Moro and communist insurgencies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Corazon_Aquino&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Peace talks with Moro and communist insurgencies")]

See also: [Moro conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moro_conflict "Moro conflict") and [Communist rebellion in the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communist_rebellion_in_the_Philippines "Communist rebellion in the Philippines")

President Aquino conducted peace talks with the [Moro National Liberation Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moro_National_Liberation_Front "Moro National Liberation Front") (MNLF), an armed [Moro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moro_people "Moro people")[Muslim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim "Muslim") insurgency group that sought to establish an independent Moro state within [Mindanao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mindanao "Mindanao"). Aquino met with MNLF leader [Nur Misuari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nur_Misuari "Nur Misuari") and various MNLF groups in [Sulu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulu "Sulu"). In 1989, the [Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autonomous_Region_in_Muslim_Mindanao "Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao") (ARMM) was created under Republic Act No. 6734 or the ARMM Organic Act, which established the Moro majority areas in the Mindanao island group as an [autonomous region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autonomous_regions_of_the_Philippines "Autonomous regions of the Philippines") with its own government.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-59) The Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao lasted from 1989 to 2019, after which it was succeeded by the [Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangsamoro_Autonomous_Region_in_Muslim_Mindanao "Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao") (BARMM).

The establishment of the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao was opposed by the [Moro Islamic Liberation Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moro_Islamic_Liberation_Front "Moro Islamic Liberation Front") (MILF), a militant splinter group from the MNLF that sought to [secede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secession "Secession") from the Philippines to establish an [Islamic state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_state "Islamic state") in Mindanao.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-60) Peace talks with MILF began in 1997 under President Fidel Ramos and violent insurgency officially continued until 2014, when peace accords were formally signed between MILF and the administration of President Benigno Aquino III that would lead to the creation of the BARMM.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-61)

The establishment of the ARMM also led to the establishment of [Abu Sayyaf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Sayyaf "Abu Sayyaf"), a [terrorist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrorism "Terrorism") group founded in 1989 by [Abdurajak Abubakar Janjalani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdurajak_Abubakar_Janjalani "Abdurajak Abubakar Janjalani") and composed of radical former members of the MNLF. Terrorist attacks by Abu Sayyaf would start in 1995 and continue to the present day, including the [2004 bombing of the MV _Superferry 14_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M/V_SuperFerry_14 "M/V SuperFerry 14") that resulted in the deaths of 116 people.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-62)

Shortly after becoming president, Aquino ordered the release of hundreds of [political prisoners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_prisoner "Political prisoner") imprisoned during the Marcos era, including [communist insurgents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communist_rebellion_in_the_Philippines "Communist rebellion in the Philippines") belonging to the [Communist Party of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communist_Party_of_the_Philippines "Communist Party of the Philippines"). These releases included leaders such as Communist Party of the Philippines founder [Jose Maria Sison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jose_Maria_Sison "Jose Maria Sison") and [New People's Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_People's_Army "New People's Army") founder [Bernabe Buscayno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernabe_Buscayno "Bernabe Buscayno"),[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-63) which the military strongly resisted.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-64) Preliminary peace talks with the CPP ended after the Mendiola Massacre on January 22, 1987, during which at least 12 farmers were killed at a protest rally.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-65)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-66)

### Closing of United States military bases

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Corazon_Aquino&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Closing of United States military bases")]

[![Image 30](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f4/Corazon_Aquino_1992.jpg/250px-Corazon_Aquino_1992.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Corazon_Aquino_1992.jpg)

Aquino addresses base workers at a rally at Remy Field concerning jobs for Filipino workers after the Americans withdraw from the U.S. facilities.

Soon after Aquino took office, several Philippine senators declared that the presence of U.S. military forces in the Philippines was an affront to national sovereignty. The senators called for the United States military to vacate [U.S. Naval Base Subic Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Naval_Base_Subic_Bay "U.S. Naval Base Subic Bay") and Clark Air Base, and Aquino opposed their demand.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-67) The United States objected by stating that they had leased the property and that the leases were still in effect.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-68) The United States stated that the facilities at [Subic Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subic_Bay "Subic Bay") were unequaled anywhere in [Southeast Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Asia "Southeast Asia") and a U.S. pullout could make all of that region of the world vulnerable to an incursion by the Soviet Union or by a resurgent Japan. Another issue with the demand was that thousands of Filipinos worked at these military facilities and they would lose their jobs if the U.S. military moved out. Aquino opposed the Senate's demand and believed that the bases should have remained. Aquino organized a protest against the pullout, which only gathered between 100,000 and 150,000 supporters, far short of the 500,000 to 1 million that had been originally expected.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-69)

The matter was still being debated when [Mount Pinatubo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Pinatubo "Mount Pinatubo") erupted in June 1991, covering the entire area with [volcanic ash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanic_ash "Volcanic ash"). Despite attempts to continue the Subic Base, Aquino finally conceded. In December 1991, the government served notice that the U.S. had to close the base by the end of 1992.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-70)

### Natural disasters and calamities

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Corazon_Aquino&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Natural disasters and calamities")]

On December 20, 1987, the [MV _Doña Paz_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MV_Do%C3%B1a_Paz "MV Doña Paz") sank after a collision with the oil tanker MV _Vector_. The final death toll exceeded 4,300 people, and the sinking has been called the deadliest peacetime maritime disaster of the 20th century.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-Hooke-71) In the aftermath, Aquino addressed the incident as "a national tragedy of harrowing proportions".[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-72)

The [1990 Luzon earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990_Luzon_earthquake "1990 Luzon earthquake") was a 7.8 [magnitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moment_magnitude_scale "Moment magnitude scale") earthquake that struck the island of [Luzon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luzon "Luzon"). It left an estimate of 1,621 people dead and massive property damage.

In 1991, a [volcanic eruption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991_eruption_of_Mount_Pinatubo "1991 eruption of Mount Pinatubo") of Mount Pinatubo, then thought to be dormant, killed around 800 people and caused widespread long-term devastation of agricultural lands in [Central Luzon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Luzon "Central Luzon").[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-73) Around 20,000 residents had to be evacuated and around 10,000 people were left homeless by the event. It was the second largest terrestrial eruption of the 20th century.

On November 1, 1991 [Tropical Storm Thelma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_Storm_Thelma "Tropical Storm Thelma") (also known as Typhoon Uring) caused massive flooding in [Ormoc City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ormoc_City "Ormoc City"), leaving around 5,000 dead in what was then considered to be the deadliest typhoon in Philippine history. On November 8, Aquino declared all of [Leyte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leyte "Leyte") a [disaster area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disaster_area "Disaster area").[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-74)

### Electrical power grid inadequacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Corazon_Aquino&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Electrical power grid inadequacy")]

During Aquino's presidency, electric [blackouts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_outage "Power outage") became common in Manila. The city experienced 7–12 hours-long blackouts, which severely affected its businesses. By the departure of Aquino in June 1992, businesses in Manila and nearby provinces had lost nearly $800 million since the preceding March.

Corazon Aquino's decision to deactivate the [Bataan Nuclear Power Plant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bataan_Nuclear_Power_Plant "Bataan Nuclear Power Plant") (BNPP), which was built during the Marcos administration, contributed to further electricity crises in the 1990s, as the 620 megawatts capacity of the plant would have been enough to cover the shortfall at that time.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-LA_Times_on_blackout-75) Critics of the BNPP had stated that the power plant was unsafe, and cited the millions of dollars in bribes paid to President Marcos to allow its construction.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-LA_Times_on_blackout-75) The administration had failed to provide for an adequate replacement for the plant before her term had completed, and President Corazon Aquino ended her term in 1992 with the country reeling under a severe power shortage crisis.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-76)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-77)

### Influence in 1992 presidential election

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Corazon_Aquino&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Influence in 1992 presidential election")]

The 1987 Constitution limited the president to a single six-year term with no possibility of re-election. As the end of her presidency drew near, close advisers and friends told Aquino that since she was not inaugurated under the 1987 Constitution, her term beginning 1986, she was still 'eligible' to seek the presidency again in the upcoming [1992 elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_Philippine_presidential_election "1992 Philippine presidential election"), the first presidential elections held under normal and peaceful circumstances since 1965. However, Aquino firmly declined the requests for her to seek reelection, citing her strong belief that the presidency was not a lifetime position.

Initially, she named [Ramon V. Mitra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_V._Mitra "Ramon V. Mitra"), Speaker of the [Philippine House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_House_of_Representatives "Philippine House of Representatives") who had been a friend of her husband, as her preferred candidate for the 1992 presidential elections. However, she later backtracked and instead supported the candidacy of General [Fidel V. Ramos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fidel_V._Ramos "Fidel V. Ramos"), who was her defense secretary and a key figure in the EDSA Revolution. Ramos had consistently stood by her government during the various coup attempts that were launched against her administration. Her sudden change of mind and withdrawal of support from Mitra drew criticism from her supporters in the liberal and [social democratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_democratic "Social democratic") sectors. Her decision also drew criticism from the Catholic Church, which questioned her support of Ramos due to him being [Protestant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestantism "Protestantism"). General Ramos won the 1992 elections with 23.58% of the total votes in a wide-open campaign.

On June 30, 1992, Corazon Aquino formally and peacefully handed over power to Fidel Ramos. On that day, Fidel V. Ramos was [inaugurated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inauguration_of_Fidel_Ramos "Inauguration of Fidel Ramos") as the twelfth president of the Philippines. After the inauguration, Aquino left the ceremony in a simple white [Toyota Crown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toyota_Crown "Toyota Crown") she had purchased, rather than the lavish government-issued [Mercedes-Benz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercedes-Benz "Mercedes-Benz") in which she and Ramos had ridden on the way to the ceremonies, to make the point that she was once again an ordinary citizen.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-78)

[![Image 31](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/66/Aquino_2003.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Aquino_2003.jpg)

Corazon Aquino speaks before the 2003 Ninoy Aquino Award ceremony at the [U.S. Embassy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embassy_of_the_United_States,_Manila "Embassy of the United States, Manila") in [Manila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manila "Manila").

### Domestic

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Corazon_Aquino&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Domestic")]

During Aquino's retirement and stay as a private citizen, she remained active in the Philippine political scene. Aquino would voice her dissent to government actions and policies that she deemed threats to the democratic foundations of the country.

In 1995, Aquino advocated for the continuation of capital punishment (since reinstated by President [Fidel V. Ramos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fidel_V._Ramos "Fidel V. Ramos") in December 1993) amidst the failure of courts to prosecute the alleged rapists in Pangasinan.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-79) By late 2000, she had changed her mind, expressing opposition to the death penalty and support for President [Joseph Estrada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Estrada "Joseph Estrada")'s attempt to repeal it.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-80)

In 1997, Aquino, together with Cardinal [Jaime Sin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaime_Sin "Jaime Sin"), led a rally opposing President Ramos' attempt to extend his term through his [proposal to amend the 1987 Constitution's restriction on presidential term limits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_reform_in_the_Philippines#Ramos_administration "Constitutional reform in the Philippines"). Ramos' proposed charter change would fail, leaving term limits and the presidential system in place.

During the [1998 Philippine presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_Philippine_presidential_election "1998 Philippine presidential election"), Aquino endorsed the candidacy of former police general and Manila Mayor [Alfredo Lim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfredo_Lim "Alfredo Lim") who is the [Liberal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Party_(Philippines) "Liberal Party (Philippines)") nominee for president. Lim would lose to Vice President [Joseph Estrada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Estrada "Joseph Estrada"), who won by a landslide.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-81) In 1999, Aquino and Cardinal Jaime Sin again worked together to oppose [a second plan to amend the Constitution to remove term limits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_reform_in_the_Philippines#Estrada_adaminsitration "Constitutional reform in the Philippines"), this time under President Estrada. President Estrada stated that his plan to amend the Constitution was intended to lift provisions that 'restrict' economic activities and investments, and Estrada denied that it was an attempt to extend his stay in office. Estrada's proposed charter change would also fail.

In 2000, Aquino joined the mounting calls for Estrada to resign from office, amid a series of corruption scandals, including strong allegations of bribery charges and gambling kickbacks. Estrada was impeached by the House of Representatives in November 2000 but acquitted by the Senate in December, which in January 2001 led to the [Second EDSA Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_EDSA_Revolution "Second EDSA Revolution"), which ousted Estrada. During the Second EDSA Revolution, Aquino enthusiastically supported the ascendancy of Vice President [Gloria Macapagal Arroyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gloria_Macapagal_Arroyo "Gloria Macapagal Arroyo") to the position of president.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-82) In the subsequent [trial of Joseph Estrada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trial_of_Joseph_Estrada "Trial of Joseph Estrada"), Estrada was acquitted of [perjury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perjury "Perjury") but found guilty of [plunder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plunder "Plunder") and sentenced to _[reclusion perpetua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reclusion\_perpetua "Reclusion perpetua")_ with the accessory [penalties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanctions_(law) "Sanctions (law)") of perpetual disqualification from [public office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_office "Public office") and [forfeiture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asset_forfeiture "Asset forfeiture") of ill-gotten wealth on September 12, 2007. Estrada was pardoned by President Macapagal-Arroyo on October 26, 2007.

In 2005, after a series of revelations and exposes that implicated President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo in [rigging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_Philippine_electoral_crisis "2005 Philippine electoral crisis") the [2004 presidential elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Philippine_general_election "2004 Philippine general election"), Aquino called on Arroyo to resign in order to prevent bloodshed, violence and further political deterioration.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-83) Aquino once again led massive street-level demonstrations, this time demanding the resignation of President Arroyo.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-84)

During the [2007 senatorial elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_Philippine_general_election "2007 Philippine general election"), Aquino actively campaigned for her only son, Benigno "Noynoy" Aquino III, who went on to win his race. Less than a year after Corazon Aquino's death in 2009, Benigno Aquino III won the [2010 Philippine presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Philippine_presidential_election "2010 Philippine presidential election") and served as the 15th president of the Philippines from 2010 to 2016.

In December 2008, Corazon Aquino publicly expressed regret for her participation in the 2001 Second EDSA Revolution, which installed Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo as president. She apologized to former President Joseph Estrada for the role she played in his ouster in 2001.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-85) Aquino's apology drew criticisms from numerous politicians.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-86) In June 2009, two months before her death, Aquino issued a public statement in which she strongly denounced and condemned the [Arroyo administration's plans of amending the 1987 Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_reform_in_the_Philippines#Arroyo_administration "Constitutional reform in the Philippines"), calling it a "shameless abuse of power".

### International

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Corazon_Aquino&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: International")]

Shortly after leaving the presidency, Aquino traveled abroad, giving speeches and lectures on issues of democracy, development, human rights, and women empowerment. At the 1994 meeting of the [UNESCO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO "UNESCO") World Commission on Culture and Development in Manila, Aquino delivered a speech urging the unconditional release of Burmese democratic leader [Aung San Suu Kyi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aung_San_Suu_Kyi "Aung San Suu Kyi") from detention.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] She petitioned for the release of Aung San Suu Kyi.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino#cite_note-87)

Aquino was a member of the [Council of Women World Leaders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Women_World_Leaders "Council of Women World Leaders"), an international organization of former and current female heads of state, from the group's inception in 1996 to her death.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

President of the Philippines from 1986 to 1992

In this [Filipino name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filipino_name "Filipino name")for [married women](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wife "Wife"), the birth [middle name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_name "Middle name") or maternal [family name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surname "Surname") is _Sumulong_, the birth surname or paternal family name is _Cojuangco_, and the [marital name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maiden_and_married_names "Maiden and married names") is _Aquino_.
